**Jonathan Nally:** In science there are lots of ways in which your life's work can be recognised. There are prizes and awards galore, important positions to be held, theories to be founded, species can be named after you, and impressive bricks and mortar facilities can be named in your honour. But for the high-achiever who has everything, it's a must to be immortalised in the sky. For instance, you can get a crater or a mountain on another planet named after you.

But when I say that you can do it, I really mean that someone else can propose your name. You can't do it because you have to have been dead for at least three years, or if you are a political figure you have to have been dead for over 200 years. And sorry, military and religious figures are out. And you must have been 'a person of high and enduring international standing'. Well, that rules me out.

But that does leave a lot of distinguished, deceased people, and there are thousands of them now commemorated on bodies in the Solar System. In fact just recently 19 more had lunar craters named after them. Most of these new ones are Nobel Prize winners. There are chemists like Carl Bosch, Fritz Haber and Victor Grignard. There are medical researchers like Theodor Kocher, who studied the thyroid, and Bernardo Houssay, the Argentinean who worked on pituitary hormones. Astronomers and even a 15th century Polish cartographer are in there too.

But the one that really caught my eye was none other than our very own Howard Walter Florey. Florey, of course, is famous for turning an obscure substance called penicillin into a new medicine during World War Two. In recognition of his work, he was knighted in 1944, jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945, and promoted to Baron in 1965. Post-war he became provost of Queen's College, Oxford, and later Chancellor of the ANU. The Howard Florey Institute in Melbourne is named in his honour, and his face was on the $50 note for many years. Prime Minister Menzies called him the 'most important man ever born in Australia'.

So why was his nationality given as British, not Australian? This was just not right. Back in Florey's day of course most Australians also considered themselves to be British. That's no longer the case, of course, but even so, while he might have been a citizen of the British Empire, his nationality definitely was Australian.

Something had to be done, so I fired off an email to the US Geological Survey, the body that maintains the master list of Solar System names. I told them that there would be trouble from down this way unless Florey's proper nationality was instated. Well, I received a nice reply pointing out that the official source documents they use list Florey as being British, apparently based on where he did the work that led to his Nobel Prize. But they did at least agree to amend the listing to 'Australian-born British pathologist'.

So, that's a partial victory at least. If you want to take it any further, you're welcome to contact me and I can put you in touch with the Maintainers of the Master List of Mixed-up Moon Monikers. Florey of course was the man who turned penicillin into a mass-produced medicine during World War Two, leading to a Noble Prize in 1945.

Well, Florey isn't the only Aussie on the Moon. According to the US Geological Survey's master list of Solar System names, there are four other Aussies immortalised on the lunar surface, or maybe five, or is it six, or even seven. The four definites are 19th and 20th century astronomers John Tebbutt, Joe Pawsey, Colin Gum and Arthur Hogg, all of whom now have craters named after them.

The fifth belongs to Antarctic explorer Douglas Mawson, who has a 132-kilometre-long ridge named after him. Although he was born in Britain, Mawson lived in Australia from the age of two.

The sixth is Sir Thomas Brisbane. Born in England, he joined the army in 1789 and served under the Duke of Wellington before leaving for Australia in 1821 to become Governor of New South Wales. He was also an astronomer and he made important contributions to the study of the southern skies. So he's sort of an honorary Aussie.

And as for the seventh...well, the list shows a crater named after Sir William Henry Bragg, a pioneer of X-ray studies and inventor of the X-ray spectrometer. Although he spent a lot of his working life in Australia and therefore can also be considered an honorary Aussie, he was actually British by birth too. So I wonder if they actually mean his son, Sir William Lawrence Bragg, who was born in Adelaide.

At the age of five, Bill junior fell off his bike and his famous dad used the then-new X-ray technique to examine his son's broken arm; its first surgical use in this country. Bragg junior followed his father into science, and together they hold the distinction of being the only father and son team to win the Nobel Prize, in 1915 for their X-ray studies of crystal structure. Bragg junior was only 25, and is still the youngest Nobel laureate.

So, whose name adorns that crater, the old Bill or the young Bill? The world needs to know. So another email was sent to the US Geological Survey, and hopefully we'll soon know if that lunar depression is actually named for the father, the son, or is the hole of both.

**Robyn Williams:** I think it's the son, Lawrence Bragg. Anyway, the Bragg Initiative bringing science to the Australian public starts in Adelaide in October this year.

# Women Scientists on the Moon: Lunar Craters Honoring Female Pioneers

Look up at the full moon on a clear night, and you’re gazing at a celestial monument to scientific achievement. The lunar surface bears the names of humanity’s greatest thinkers, immortalized in the craters formed by ancient impacts. Yet among the 1,586 named features on the Moon, only 31 honor women. These **women scientists on the moon** represent less than 2% of all named lunar features, a stark reminder of how recently women gained recognition in science.

Each **lunar crater named after women** tells a story of breakthrough discoveries, persistent determination, and barriers overcome. From Hypatia of ancient Alexandria to modern astronauts, these pioneers transformed mathematics, astronomy, physics, and space exploration. Their names now shine permanently on Earth’s nearest celestial neighbor, visible reminders that scientific genius knows no gender.

This Women’s History Month, we explore the remarkable women whose contributions earned them this astronomical honor. Their craters dot both the familiar near side and mysterious far side of the Moon, each one a testament to discoveries that expanded human knowledge and inspired future generations of scientists.

## A Celestial Hall of Fame With Few Women

### How Lunar Features Get Their Names

The International Astronomical Union (IAU) has governed the naming of celestial features since 1919. For lunar craters, the tradition began centuries earlier when astronomers like Giovanni Riccioli started assigning names to visible features. The convention established that **lunar craters honor deceased scientists, scholars, explorers, and astronauts** who made significant contributions to their fields.

The process isn’t automatic. Proposals must demonstrate the individual’s lasting impact on science. The IAU’s Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature reviews submissions, considering factors like the significance of contributions, international representation, and whether similar names might cause confusion. Once approved, these names become permanent, surviving longer than any earthly monument.

### The Stark Gender Gap

Of approximately 1,586 named lunar craters, only 31 commemorate women. This 2% representation reflects historical realities: for most of recorded history, women were systematically excluded from universities, scientific societies, and professional research positions. Many brilliant **female astronomers** and scientists worked without recognition, their discoveries attributed to male colleagues or simply forgotten.

The distribution across the Moon tells another story. The near side, visible from Earth and mapped earliest, contains 14 craters honoring women. The far side, invisible from Earth until photographed by spacecraft in 1959, features 17. This slightly higher representation on the far side reflects more recent naming efforts as attitudes gradually shifted toward recognizing women’s contributions.

### Recent Progress and Ongoing Efforts

Most women-honoring craters received their names relatively recently. While male scientists like Copernicus, Kepler, and Newton have had lunar craters since the 1600s-1700s, many women’s names weren’t added until the 20th century. As awareness grew of women’s historical contributions and contemporary achievements, the IAU began approving more proposals recognizing female scientists.

Today, organizations and individuals continue proposing names of deserving women scientists for unnamed lunar features. Each approval represents not just historical recognition but inspiration for young women considering scientific careers, showing that their contributions will be remembered and celebrated.

## Meet the Women on the Moon

### Ancient Scholars and Early Pioneers

#### Hypatia (c. 350-415 CE)

The **Hypatia crater**, located on the Moon’s near side, honors one of history’s first documented female mathematicians and astronomers. Teaching in Alexandria, Egypt, Hypatia wrote commentaries on classical mathematical texts and built astronomical instruments. Her murder by a mob in 415 CE symbolized the destruction of Alexandria’s intellectual golden age. The crater bearing her name, approximately 41 kilometers in diameter, ensures this pioneering scholar’s legacy endures. Our [hand-drawn Hypatia poster](https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/product/hypatia-poster/ "Hypatia Poster") celebrates her famous quote: “Reserve your right to think, for even to think wrongly is better than not to think at all.”

#### Caroline Herschel (1750-1848)

Crater Herschel honors the astronomer who discovered eight comets and compiled comprehensive catalogs of celestial objects. Working alongside her brother William, Caroline became a pioneering astronomer in her own right, earning recognition from Britain’s Royal Astronomical Society. The 13-kilometer crater on the far side of the Moon commemorates her meticulous observations that advanced 18th-century astronomy.

### Nobel Laureates and Physics Pioneers

#### Marie Curie (1867-1934)

The Sklodowska crater (Marie Curie’s maiden name) on the far side honors the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her groundbreaking research on radioactivity, documented in her [doctoral thesis “Recherches sur les substances radioactives”](https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/product/marie-curie-thesis/ "Marie Curie's Thesis"), established foundations for nuclear physics. The 127-kilometer crater befits her towering contributions to science.

#### Lise Meitner (1878-1968)

Crater Meitner commemorates the physicist who discovered nuclear fission. Despite her critical role in this breakthrough, her male colleague Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize alone, one of science’s most notorious oversights. The 87-kilometer crater on the far side ensures history remembers her essential contributions to atomic physics.

### Mathematicians Who Changed the Field

#### Emmy Noether (1882-1935)

The Noether crater honors the mathematician Einstein called “the most significant creative mathematical genius” since women’s higher education began. Her theorem connecting symmetries and conservation laws became fundamental to modern physics. The 67-kilometer crater on the far side represents her revolutionary impact on abstract algebra and theoretical physics.

#### Sofia Kovalevskaya (1850-1891)

Crater Kovalevskaya recognizes the first woman to obtain a doctorate in mathematics and the first female professor in Northern Europe. Her work on differential equations and mechanics advanced mathematical analysis. The 115-kilometer far side crater commemorates her persistence in pursuing mathematics despite pervasive discrimination.

### Astronomers and Space Pioneers

#### Valentina Tereshkova (1937-present)

Although still living, Tereshkova has a crater proposed in her honor for being the first woman in space (1963). Her Vostok 6 mission made her a global icon, proving women could withstand spaceflight’s demands. While IAU typically honors only deceased individuals, her historic achievement may warrant exception.

#### Williamina Fleming (1857-1911)

Crater Fleming honors the astronomer who classified thousands of stars and discovered numerous nebulae while working at Harvard Observatory. Starting as a maid and becoming a renowned astronomer, her story exemplifies how talent overcomes barriers. The 106-kilometer crater acknowledges her stellar classification system still used today.

## Why Lunar Recognition Matters Today

The small number of **women on the moon** isn’t just historical curiosity; it reflects ongoing challenges in achieving gender equity in STEM fields. While formal barriers have largely fallen, women remain underrepresented in physics, mathematics, and engineering. Visible recognition matters because it:

Organizations now actively work to identify deserving women scientists for unnamed lunar features. Recent efforts focus on lesser-known pioneers whose contributions were overlooked or attributed to male colleagues. Each new crater name approved represents progress toward equitable recognition.

The stark numerical disparity also sparks important conversations. Why are there so few women? Not because women lacked ability, but because they faced institutional barriers that made scientific careers nearly impossible. Understanding this context transforms the 31 craters from mere names into monuments to persistence against systematic discrimination.

For educators, the **women scientists moon craters** provide tangible teaching tools. Students can locate these craters through telescopes or lunar maps, connecting abstract history lessons to visible celestial features. Each crater becomes a starting point for exploring that scientist’s achievements and the obstacles she overcame.

## Celebrating Women Scientists Through Lunar Cartography

Our [Women on the Moon poster set](https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/product/women-on-the-moon-posters/ "Women on the Moon Posters") beautifully maps all 31 lunar features honoring women scientists. These two A2-sized prints show both the near side (14 women pioneers including Hypatia and Caroline Herschel) and far side (17 luminaries such as Marie Curie, Emmy Noether, and astronauts from Space Shuttle missions). Each crater is labeled with the scientist’s name and lifespan, making these posters both decorative art and educational resources.

Perfect for classrooms, offices, or home studies, these maps inspire conversations about women’s contributions to science while serving as functional lunar reference guides. The posters document not just the craters but the remarkable women whose discoveries in mathematics, astronomy, physics, and space exploration earned them this celestial honor.

Complement these maps with our [Hypatia poster](https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/product/hypatia-poster/ "Hypatia Poster") or Marie Curie’s [original doctoral thesis](https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/product/marie-curie-thesis/ "Marie Curie's Thesis") to explore specific pioneers’ contributions in greater depth, creating a comprehensive celebration of women in science.

## Looking Up, Moving Forward

Every time you look at the Moon, you’re seeing a permanent record of scientific achievement. Among those countless craters, 31 bear names of women who refused to accept that intellectual pursuits belonged only to men. From ancient Hypatia to modern astronauts, these pioneers proved that scientific genius transcends gender barriers.

The small percentage reminds us how recently women gained access to scientific education and professional recognition. But each crater also represents hope: as we add more women’s names to lunar features, we document growing acknowledgment that science advances fastest when all talented minds contribute freely.

These women reached for the stars. Now their names shine among them forever.

**Fischer** is a [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies in the northeastern part of the interior floor of [Mendeleev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendeleev_(crater) "Mendeleev (crater)"), a huge [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain"). This feature is located on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon") relative to the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"), and can only be viewed from a [spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft").[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3)

This crater has a slender, circular rim and an interior that has the same [albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") as the surrounding surface. There is a smaller impact crater within the interior, adjacent to the northwestern inner wall. The rim and the floor of Fischer are pitted by several tiny craterlets.[[4]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-4)

The crater is named after two German [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry") laureates: chemist [Emil Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Fischer "Emil Fischer") (1852–1919) and organic chemist [Hans Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Fischer "Hans Fischer") (1881–1945).[[5]](#cite_note-Cocks_1995-5) Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1976.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)
